summary: A short note on how to write math-like descriptions in specifications. When a function uses two formulas for adjoining domains but is continuous at the boundary, the author describes it in a particular form. It also replaces the correction in RFC 132 and updates RFC 107.

plainLanguage.summary: A little advice on writing explanations clearly: if a rule changes at one point but still joins smoothly, here is a neat way to write it down.

subtitle: A one-paragraph note on how to write a piecewise function so that nobody can misread it.

tldr.problem: A function sometimes needs two formulas for adjoining domains even though it is continuous at the boundary point, and the usual way of writing it can look ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: The author writes the function as f(x) = f1(x) for x =< a and f(x) = f2(x) for x >= a, letting the two domains overlap at the boundary point a.
tldr.outcome: The overlap is harmless because f1(a) = f2(a), so no semantic ambiguity obtains. The RFC obsoletes RFC 132 and updates RFC 107.

today: RFC 154 is an early ARPANET-era note whose status is listed as Unknown. It obsoletes RFC 132 and updates RFC 107, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: The Problem Being Described
sections.content:
RFC 154 is a one-page note by S. Crocker, dated 12 May 1971, titled Exposition Style. It calls its subject a pedagogical device, a way of teaching or describing a function.

The function it has in mind is drawn as a graph: a line that runs flat and then, at a point marked a on the horizontal axis, bends upward. Two formulae, f1 and f2, are needed because each one covers a different adjoining domain, but the function is continuous at the boundary point.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a slide that is flat for a while and then goes up like a ramp. You need one rule for the flat part and another rule for the ramp.

sections.title: The Suggested Form
sections.content:
The author usually writes the description with two lines:

f(x) = f1(x) for x =< a
f(x) = f2(x) for x >= a

Both lines include the boundary point a, so the two domains overlap there.
sections.plainLanguage: You write one rule for everything up to the meeting spot and another rule for everything from the meeting spot onward.

sections.title: Why the Overlap Is Safe
sections.content:
The RFC points out that an astute reader will notice the overlap. Normally two formulas claiming the same point could disagree about its value.

Here they cannot, because f1(a) = f2(a). Whichever line a reader applies at a, the answer is the same, so in the RFC's words no semantic ambiguity obtains.
sections.plainLanguage: If two friends both say a spot is theirs but they agree on what is there, nobody gets confused.
